```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")

widget <- function(file) htmltools::includeHTML(file.path("widgets", file))
f2 <- function(v) formatC(round(v, 2) + 0, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)
f4 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 4)
sci <- function(v, d = 1) {
  e <- floor(log10(v))
  paste0(formatC(v / 10^e, format = "f", digits = d), " \\times 10^{", e, "}")
}
```

```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5,
       col = if (identical(highlight, "DATA")) "lightskyblue1" else NA)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}
```

R code from this page is also in the
[companion script](lecture_notes/CODE_Week6_LikelihoodAndPowerAnalysis.R).
No packages beyond base R are needed.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
sections 6.1-6.2.1 and 6.3.1 (likelihood and maximum likelihood,
pp. 227-236 and 243-247) and 5.3 (power analysis, pp. 209-226).

# Likelihood and maximum likelihood estimation {#likelihood}

Simulation runs a model forward: choose the parameters, then generate
data. Inference runs it backward: the data are fixed, and the question
is which parameter values could have produced them. This part defines
the likelihood, explains why we work with its negative logarithm, and
shows three ways to find the parameter values that make the data most
probable.

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-likelihood, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("FIT")
```

A data-generating model (the MODELS box) says how data arise for given
parameter values. The FIT step confronts that model with real data.
Nearly every fitting method in this course, from maximum likelihood to
Markov chain Monte Carlo, is built on one quantity: the **likelihood**,
the probability of the data we actually observed under a fully
specified model (Bolker p. 228).

## 2. WOD: writing the likelihood {#wod-likelihood}

The WOD (a short warm-up exercise at the start of class) asked students
to write a likelihood from scratch. Four sage-grouse nests were
monitored; each either hatched at least one egg ($y_i = 1$) or failed
($y_i = 0$):

```{r nest-table, echo=FALSE}
nests <- data.frame(Nest = 1:4, Cover = c(30, 20, 10, 30), Outcome = c(1, 1, 0, 1))
knitr::kable(nests, col.names = c("Nest", "Sagebrush cover (%)",
                                  "Outcome (1 = hatched, 0 = failed)"),
             align = "c")
```

If every nest has the same success probability $p$, one nest's outcome
has probability $P(y \mid p) = p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}$: $p$ when $y = 1$ and
$1 - p$ when $y = 0$. Read the other way, with the outcome fixed and
$p$ allowed to vary, the same formula is the **likelihood** of $p$.
The likelihood is written as a function of the parameter alone,
$\mathcal{L}_1(p)$, with no conditioning bar, because it is not a
probability distribution over $p$. The subscript counts the
observations.

If the nests are independent, the probability of all four outcomes is
the product of the four probabilities:

$$\mathcal{L}_4(p) = \prod_{i=1}^{4} p^{y_i}(1-p)^{1-y_i} = p^3 (1-p).$$

```{r nest-likelihood, fig.height=3.6}
p_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.005)
lik_nests <- function(p) p^3 * (1 - p)
p_three <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(p_grid, lik_nests(p_grid), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Nest success probability, p", ylab = "Likelihood")
points(p_three, lik_nests(p_three), pch = 16, cex = 1.2)
```

The dots are the values the WOD asked for: $3/256$, $16/256$, and
$27/256$. The WOD went on to let $p$ depend on sagebrush cover through a
logistic function (see the [logistic regression
section](Week7_IntervalsAndBayes.html#logistic) on the next page).

> **Question:** Add up the three likelihood values. Do they sum to 1?
> Should they?

## 3. From likelihood to negative log-likelihood {#nll}

Take counts of active pika haypiles in six talus plots of equal size:
2, 5, 3, 0, 4, and 4. Model each count as Poisson with an unknown mean
$\lambda$ (haypiles per plot). The likelihood is the product of the six
Poisson probabilities:

$$\mathcal{L}_6(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{6} P(y_i \mid \lambda)
  = \prod_{i=1}^{6} \frac{\lambda^{y_i} e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}.$$

In practice we almost never work with this product directly. We take
its logarithm and change the sign:

$$\ell_6(\lambda) = \log \mathcal{L}_6(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{6} \log P(y_i \mid \lambda),
  \qquad \text{NLL}(\lambda) = -\ell_6(\lambda).$$

- **Why the log?** A product of many numbers below 1 shrinks toward
  zero. The WOD imagined 1,852 nests, each with likelihood about 0.5:
  their product is about $10^{`r round(1852 * log10(0.5))`}$, far below
  the smallest positive number a computer can store, so R rounds it to
  exactly 0. The sum of the logs is `r f2(1852 * log(0.5))`, an ordinary
  number. Sums are also much easier to differentiate than products.
- **Why the minus sign?** Optimization software, including R's
  `optim()`, is written to *minimize* a function. Flipping the sign
  turns "find the highest point of the likelihood" into "find the lowest
  point of the negative log-likelihood (NLL)." There is no deeper
  reason.

```{r pika-nll, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
haypiles <- c(2, 5, 3, 0, 4, 4)

nll_pois <- function(lambda, y) {
  -sum(dpois(y, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

lambda_grid <- seq(0.5, 7, by = 0.01)
lik_vals <- sapply(lambda_grid, function(l) prod(dpois(haypiles, l)))
nll_vals <- sapply(lambda_grid, nll_pois, y = haypiles)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(lambda_grid, lik_vals, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "lambda (haypiles per plot)", ylab = "Likelihood")
abline(v = 3, lty = 3)
plot(lambda_grid, nll_vals, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "lambda (haypiles per plot)", ylab = "Negative log-likelihood")
abline(v = 3, lty = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The widget shows where the product comes from. At each candidate mean,
the left panel draws the Poisson probabilities, and the red dots mark
the probability of each observed count. The likelihood multiplies the
heights of the red dots; the right panel shows the NLL across all
candidate means.

```{r likelihood-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("likelihood_product.html")
```

> **Question:** Slide $\lambda$ from 1.5 to 3 to 6. Which observed
> count is most to blame for the poor likelihood at each end? Then
> switch to "Four times as many plots." What happens to the likelihood
> at the MLE, and what happens to the shape of the NLL curve?

## 4. The maximum likelihood estimate {#mle}

The **maximum likelihood estimate** (MLE) is the parameter value that
makes the observed data most probable:

$$\hat{\lambda} = \arg\max_{\lambda} \mathcal{L}_6(\lambda)
  = \arg\min_{\lambda} \text{NLL}(\lambda).$$

Both panels above peak (or bottom out) at the same place, because taking
the log never changes which of two numbers is larger. For the pikas,
$\hat\lambda = 3$.

What matters is *where* the peak is, not how high it is. The likelihood
at the MLE is only about $`r sci(prod(dpois(haypiles, 3)))`$, and it
would be smaller still with more plots: each extra observation
multiplies in another probability below 1. A small likelihood is not a
sign of a bad model. Only comparisons between parameter values (or
models) on the same data carry information.

There are three ways to find the MLE (Bolker pp. 229-231 works through
the first and third for a binomial example):

1. **Calculus.** Set the derivative of $\ell(\lambda)$ to zero and
   solve. For the Poisson this gives $\hat\lambda = \bar y$, the sample
   mean. Exact, but it works only when the algebra cooperates.
2. **Grid search.** Compute the NLL at many candidate values and keep
   the smallest. Easy to understand and check, but slow, and hopeless
   with many parameters: 100 values for each of 5 parameters is
   $100^5 = 10^{10}$ evaluations.
3. **A numerical optimizer.** Start from a guess and move downhill until
   the NLL stops improving. R's `optim()` needs the NLL function and a
   starting value.

```{r pika-three-ways}
lambda_grid[which.min(nll_vals)]           # grid search

fit_pika <- optim(par = 2, fn = nll_pois, y = haypiles,
                  method = "Brent", lower = 0.01, upper = 20)
fit_pika$par                               # optimizer
fit_pika$value                             # NLL at the MLE
```

`method = "Brent"` is `optim()`'s option for a single parameter. With
two or more parameters the default method (Nelder-Mead, described on the
[MCMC page](Week9_MCMC.html#nelder-mead)) works.

```{r pika-grid-vs-optim, fig.height=3.6}
coarse <- seq(1, 6, by = 0.5)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(lambda_grid, nll_vals, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "lambda (haypiles per plot)", ylab = "Negative log-likelihood")
points(coarse, sapply(coarse, nll_pois, y = haypiles), pch = 16)
points(fit_pika$par, fit_pika$value, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3, col = "red")
legend("top", c("grid points", "optim() result"), pch = c(16, 4),
       col = c("black", "red"), bty = "n")
```

## Discussion

1. A labmate fits the Poisson model to the pika counts and reports that
   the likelihood at the MLE is only
   $`r sci(prod(dpois(haypiles, 3)))`$, so "the model must fit badly."
   Is that a fair conclusion? What would you look at instead?
2. Multiplying the six probabilities assumes the plots are independent.
   Give an ecological reason that could fail for neighboring talus
   plots. Would it change the MLE, our confidence in it, or both?

## Bonus: fitting by simulation {#by-eye}

Before likelihood, one way to fit a model is by trial and error with
simulation: guess the parameters, simulate many data sets, and see
whether the real data look like they could have come from the same
model. The data here are R's built-in `trees` data set: diameter
(labeled `Girth` in the data; inches, at 4.5 ft) and timber volume
(cubic feet) of 31 felled black cherry trees. A power law, the usual
form for allometry, is a natural model:

$$V_i \sim \text{Normal}\left(a D_i^{\,b},\ \sigma\right).$$

```{r trees-setup}
data(trees)
diam <- trees$Girth      # diameter in inches (mislabeled "Girth")
vol <- trees$Volume      # cubic feet

power_curve <- function(d, a, b) a * d^b

# 95% range of volumes simulated at each diameter, for parameters (a, b, sigma)
sim_band <- function(par, d_seq, n_sims = 1000) {
  sims <- replicate(n_sims, rnorm(length(d_seq), power_curve(d_seq, par[1], par[2]), par[3]))
  apply(sims, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
}
```

```{r trees-by-eye, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.4}
set.seed(6)
d_seq <- seq(8, 21, length.out = 50)
guesses <- list(c(0.1, 2.2, 3), c(0.5, 1.6, 3), c(0.5, 1.6, 15))

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
for (g in guesses) {
  band <- sim_band(g, d_seq)
  plot(diam, vol, pch = 16, ylim = c(-20, 110), xlab = "Diameter (in)",
       ylab = "Volume (cubic ft)",
       main = paste0("a = ", g[1], ", b = ", g[2], ", sigma = ", g[3]), cex.main = 1)
  polygon(c(d_seq, rev(d_seq)), c(band[1, ], rev(band[2, ])),
          col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25), border = NA)
  lines(d_seq, power_curve(d_seq, g[1], g[2]), lwd = 2, col = "steelblue4")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The first guess puts most trees inside the 95% band. The second runs
too high for the smallest trees and too low for the largest. The third
"fixes" the second by making the noise huge.

> **Question:** Why not simply increase $\sigma$ until every point falls
> inside the band?

Likelihood replaces judging by eye with one number per guess. The NLLs
for the three guesses:

```{r nll-power-def}
nll_power <- function(par, d, v) {
  -sum(dnorm(v, mean = power_curve(d, par[1], par[2]), sd = par[3], log = TRUE))
}
```

```{r trees-guess-nll}
sapply(guesses, nll_power, d = diam, v = vol)
```

The first guess has by far the lowest NLL. Widening the band in the
third guess doesn't rescue the badly shaped curve: when the
distribution is spread over a wide range, including impossible negative
volumes, every observed volume gets a low density. The [next
part](#lab5) fits this model properly.

# Fitting a model with several parameters {#lab5}

These topics opened the lab on maximum likelihood. They cover the
pieces needed to fit any model by likelihood: densities for continuous
data, writing a negative log-likelihood function, starting values and
`optim()`, and checking that the fit makes sense. The example is the
black cherry tree data from the [bonus section above](#by-eye).

## 1. Likelihood for continuous data {#continuous}

```{r trees-plot, fig.height=3.8}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(diam, vol, pch = 16, xlab = "Diameter (in)", ylab = "Volume (cubic ft)")
```

Why a power law? A tree trunk is roughly a cylinder or cone, with volume
proportional to diameter$^2 \times$ height. If height didn't change
with diameter, $b$ would be 2. Wider trees also tend to be taller, so we
expect $b$ somewhat above 2.

For continuous data, the probability of any exact value is zero, so the
likelihood uses the probability **density** instead (Bolker p. 229).
For the first tree (diameter `r diam[1]` in, volume `r vol[1]` cubic
ft), with parameters close to the best fit:

```{r one-tree, fig.height=3.4}
par_try <- c(a = 0.087, b = 2.24, sigma = 3.2)
mu_1 <- power_curve(diam[1], par_try["a"], par_try["b"])   # expected volume
dens_1 <- dnorm(vol[1], mean = mu_1, sd = par_try["sigma"])
c(expected = unname(mu_1), density = unname(dens_1))

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
curve(dnorm(x, mu_1, par_try["sigma"]), from = 0, to = 22, lwd = 2,
      xlab = "Volume (cubic ft) of a tree with diameter 8.3 in", ylab = "Probability density")
abline(v = vol[1], col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

The likelihood of this one observation is the height of the curve where
the red line crosses it, `r f3(dens_1)`.

- A density isn't a probability, and it depends on the units. Measure
  volume in cubic meters instead of cubic feet, and the same tree's
  density is
  `r f2(dnorm(vol[1] * 0.0283168, mu_1 * 0.0283168, par_try["sigma"] * 0.0283168))`.
  The change is the same for every parameter value, though, so it
  doesn't move the MLE or change any comparison between parameter
  values.
- For all 31 trees, the likelihood is the product of 31 densities,
  $`r sci(prod(dnorm(vol, power_curve(diam, 0.087, 2.24), 3.2)))`$,
  and the log-likelihood is the sum of their logs,
  `r f2(sum(dnorm(vol, power_curve(diam, 0.087, 2.24), 3.2, log = TRUE)))`.

## 2. Writing a negative log-likelihood function {#nll-function}

Every NLL function has the same structure (Bolker pp. 243-244):

- **Input:** a vector of candidate parameter values (and the data).
- **Deterministic part:** compute each observation's expected value from
  the parameters (here, $a D_i^b$).
- **Stochastic part:** compute the log probability (or log density) of
  each observation, given its expected value and any noise parameters.
- **Output:** the negative of their sum.

`nll_power()`, written in the [bonus section](#by-eye), follows this
pattern:

```{r nll-function-show, ref.label="nll-power-def", eval=FALSE}
```

```{r nll-function}
nll_power(par_try, d = diam, v = vol)
```

Check a new NLL function on values you can verify another way, for
example against a one-observation calculation like the one in
[section 1](#continuous), before handing it to an optimizer.

## 3. Starting values and optim() {#optim}

`optim()` needs a starting guess for every parameter. It doesn't have
to be good, but it should be in the right neighborhood, especially for
nonlinear models. Two strategies (Bolker uses both on pp. 244 and
246):

- **Use what the parameters mean.** $b \approx 2$ from the geometry
  above. Then the first tree, volume `r vol[1]` at diameter `r diam[1]`,
  suggests $a \approx `r vol[1]` / `r diam[1]`^2 =
  `r f2(vol[1] / diam[1]^2)`$. The points scatter a few cubic feet
  around any smooth curve, so $\sigma \approx 3$.
- **Plot the guess against the data**, and adjust until it is close.

```{r trees-start, fig.height=3.8}
start <- c(a = 0.15, b = 2, sigma = 3)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(diam, vol, pch = 16, xlab = "Diameter (in)", ylab = "Volume (cubic ft)")
curve(power_curve(x, start["a"], start["b"]), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

The guess runs a little high for large trees, but it is close enough
for `optim()`:

```{r trees-optim}
fit_trees <- optim(par = start, fn = nll_power, d = diam, v = vol)
fit_trees$par           # MLEs of a, b, and sigma
fit_trees$value         # NLL at the MLE
fit_trees$convergence   # 0 means optim() thinks it converged
```

- `optim()` passes the extra arguments (`d` and `v`) on to `nll_power()`.
- **Always check `convergence`**, and try a second starting point. A
  different start that reaches the same answer is reassuring:

```{r trees-optim-start2}
round(optim(c(a = 0.05, b = 2.5, sigma = 5), nll_power, d = diam, v = vol)$par, 3)
```

- The estimate $\hat b = `r f2(fit_trees$par["b"])`$ is above 2, as the
  geometry suggested.
- $\sigma$ must be positive. A common trick is to estimate
  $\log \sigma$ instead and exponentiate inside the NLL function, so
  the optimizer can never try a negative value.

## 4. Checking the fit {#check-fit}

An MLE is the best parameter set *for this model*. It says nothing about
whether the model describes the data well. Bolker (p. 245) recommends
always plotting the fit. Simulating many data sets from the fitted
model, as in the [bonus section](#by-eye), shows the range of data the
model expects:

```{r trees-check, fig.height=4}
set.seed(7)
band_fit <- sim_band(fit_trees$par, d_seq)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(diam, vol, pch = 16, xlab = "Diameter (in)", ylab = "Volume (cubic ft)",
     ylim = c(0, 85))
polygon(c(d_seq, rev(d_seq)), c(band_fit[1, ], rev(band_fit[2, ])),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25), border = NA)
curve(power_curve(x, fit_trees$par["a"], fit_trees$par["b"]), add = TRUE,
      lwd = 2, col = "steelblue4")
```

```{r trees-exp, include=FALSE}
nll_exp <- function(par, d, v) -sum(dnorm(v, par[1] * exp(par[2] * d), par[3], log = TRUE))
fit_exp <- optim(c(5, 0.15, 3), nll_exp, d = diam, v = vol)
```

> **Question:** The model assumes the same noise ($\sigma$) for small
> and large trees. Does the plot support that? If not, what kind of
> distribution might describe volume better?

> **Question:** The same recipe fits any other curve. An exponential
> curve, $V = a e^{bD}$, has its best NLL at `r f2(fit_exp$value)`,
> compared with `r f2(fit_trees$value)` for the power law. Is a
> difference that size enough to prefer the power law? What else would
> you want to know?

## Bonus: deviance and goodness of fit {#deviance}

The NLL compares parameter values for one model, but on its own it
doesn't say whether the model fits. One classical check compares the
model with a **saturated** model, which gives every observation its own
parameter and so fits perfectly. For the pikas, the saturated Poisson
model sets each plot's mean equal to its own count.

The **deviance** is twice the difference in NLL between the fitted and
saturated models. If the model is correct, the deviance approximately
follows a $\chi^2$ distribution (see the [likelihood ratio
section](Week7_IntervalsAndBayes.html#lr-interval) on the next page),
with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of
parameters, here $6 - 1 = 5$:

```{r pika-deviance}
nll_saturated <- -sum(dpois(haypiles, lambda = haypiles, log = TRUE))
deviance_pika <- 2 * (nll_pois(3, haypiles) - nll_saturated)
c(deviance = deviance_pika, df = 5,
  p_value = pchisq(deviance_pika, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE))
```

The expected value of a $\chi^2$ distribution is its degrees of freedom,
so for a model that fits, the deviance divided by its degrees of freedom
should be near 1. Here it is `r f2(deviance_pika / 5)`, and the
$p$-value of `r f2(pchisq(deviance_pika, 5, lower.tail = FALSE))` gives
no strong evidence against the Poisson model. That is why model
summaries in R (for example, from `glm()`) report the residual deviance
and its degrees of freedom. With only six small counts the $\chi^2$
approximation is rough, so a simulation check like the [one
above](#check-fit) is worth doing too.

# A power analysis in code {#power}

This part builds a power analysis for a wildlife monitoring program,
one tested function at a time. A power analysis uses simulated data
from a model we specify to ask how often a study design would detect an
effect of a given size, before anyone collects data. The design
question: how much survey effort, and how often, does it take to detect
a 25% decline in a rare toad population?

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-power, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("DATA")
```

The dashed side box is study design. A fully specified model (MODELS)
can generate data for any proposed sampling plan, and analyzing those
simulated data sets the way we'd analyze the real ones (FIT) shows how
often the plan would work. Bolker's section 5.3 works through power
analysis this way.

The code below also shows a way of working that applies to any
simulation or likelihood code: write one small function at a time, and
test each one against a case where you already know the answer before
building on it.

## 2. WOD: find the bugs {#wod-bugs}

The WOD showed two short functions, each with one bug. Both run without
an error. `detect_prob(k)` should give the probability that $k$
person-days of searching detect an animal that each person-day detects
with probability 0.02, which is $1 - (1 - 0.02)^k$. `sim_detect()`
should simulate many surveys (3 visits each, detection probability 0.4
per visit) and return the fraction with at least one detection.

```{r wod-buggy, eval=FALSE}
detect_prob <- function(k, pobs = 0.02) {
  1 - pobs^k
}

sim_detect <- function(R = 1000, visits = 3, p = 0.4) {
  detected <- logical(R)
  for (i in seq_len(R)) {
    n_det <- rbinom(1, size = visits, prob = p)
    detected <- n_det > 0
  }
  mean(detected)
}
```

> **Question:** Find each bug. For one of them, what quick check (one
> line of code and the answer you'd expect) would have caught it?

## 3. The design problem {#design-problem}

A state wildlife agency is planning a 25-year monitoring program for a
rare, secretive toad. The management goal is a program with **at least a
75% chance of detecting a decline of 25% or more over 25 years**.

- **Population:** $N_0 = 1000$ toads in year 0, declining by the same
  proportion each year, $N_t = N_0 \lambda^t$ with
  $\lambda = 0.75^{1/25}$, so $N_{25} = 750$.
- **Surveys:** each person-day of searching detects a given toad with
  probability 0.02. A survey uses $k$ person-days and is repeated every
  $s$ years, starting in year 1. Each survey's count is
  Binomial($N_t$, detection probability).
- **Analysis:** fit a straight line to log(count) against year. A
  decline is detected if the slope is negative **and** its $p$-value is
  at most 0.05. (Fitting on the log scale gives an unbiased estimate of
  the yearly rate of decline.)
- **Costs:** \$200 per person-day, plus \$2,000 for each survey
  expedition.

What is the cheapest design that meets the goal?

## 4. Building and testing the pieces {#pieces}

**Detection probability.** A toad is missed on one person-day with
probability $1 - 0.02$, and on all $k$ person-days with probability
$(1 - 0.02)^k$, so a survey detects it with probability
$q(k) = 1 - (1 - 0.02)^k$.

```{r detect-prob}
detect_prob <- function(k, pobs = 0.02) {
  1 - (1 - pobs)^k
}
detect_prob(1)   # one person-day should equal pobs
detect_prob(3)
```

**True abundance.** Test it with a vector of years, since that's how the
next function will call it:

```{r true-abundance}
true_abundance <- function(t, N0 = 1000, lambda = 0.75^(1/25)) {
  N0 * lambda^t
}
true_abundance(c(0, 25))   # should return 1000 and 750 together
```

**Simulated counts.** One binomial draw per survey year:

```{r simulate-counts}
simulate_counts <- function(t_survey, k, N0 = 1000, lambda = 0.75^(1/25),
                            pobs = 0.02) {
  N_t <- true_abundance(t_survey, N0, lambda)
  rbinom(length(t_survey), size = round(N_t), prob = detect_prob(k, pobs))
}
set.seed(11)
counts <- simulate_counts(1:25, k = 3)
length(counts)   # should be 25
```

```{r simulate-counts-plot, fig.height=3.4}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(1:25, counts, pch = 16, xlab = "Year", ylab = "Count",
     ylim = c(0, max(counts) * 1.1))
```

`round()` is there because a binomial's number of trials must be a
whole number. The counts sit far below the true abundance (1000 falling
to 750) because each survey detects fewer than 6% of the toads.

**The decision rule.** A negative slope *and* $p \le 0.05$:

```{r detect-decline}
detect_decline <- function(t_survey, counts, alpha = 0.05) {
  s <- summary(lm(log(counts) ~ t_survey))$coefficients[2, ]
  unname(s[1] < 0 && s[4] <= alpha)
}
detect_decline(1:25, counts)
```

A test with a known answer: simulate a stable population
($\lambda = 1$) many times. A significant slope should turn up about 5%
of the time, but only about half of those slopes are negative, so the
rule should report a decline about 2.5% of the time.

```{r detect-decline-null}
set.seed(12)
null_hits <- replicate(1000, {
  detect_decline(1:25, simulate_counts(1:25, 3, lambda = 1))
})
mean(null_hits)
```

## 5. Power across designs {#design-space}

`estimate_power()` simulates `R` monitoring programs for one design and
returns the fraction that detect the decline:

```{r estimate-power}
estimate_power <- function(k, s, R = 1000, lambda = 0.75^(1/25),
                           alpha = 0.05) {
  t_survey <- seq(1, 25, by = s)
  mean(replicate(R, {
    counts <- simulate_counts(t_survey, k, lambda = lambda)
    detect_decline(t_survey, counts, alpha)
  }))
}
set.seed(14)
estimate_power(3, 1, lambda = 1)   # false-decline rate
estimate_power(3, 1)               # power
```

Before trusting a power estimate, check that the same function gives
the expected false-decline rate (about 0.025) when there is no decline.

Now every combination of $k$ from 1 to 15 and $s$ from 1 to 5:

```{r power-grid}
set.seed(746)
grid <- expand.grid(k = 1:15, s = 1:5)
grid$power <- mapply(estimate_power, grid$k, grid$s,
                     MoreArgs = list(R = 1000))
```

```{r power-grid-plot, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 15), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Person-days per survey, k",
     ylab = "Estimated power")
abline(h = 0.75, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
for (ss in 1:5) {
  lines(grid$k[grid$s == ss], grid$power[grid$s == ss], col = ss, lwd = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("s =", 1:5), col = 1:5, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

Power rises with effort per survey and falls with the interval between
surveys. Next, the cost of each design and the cheapest ones that meet
the goal:

```{r power-cost}
cost_of <- function(k, s) length(seq(1, 25, by = s)) * (2000 + 200 * k)
grid$cost <- mapply(cost_of, grid$k, grid$s)
ok <- grid[grid$power >= 0.75, ]
head(ok[order(ok$cost), ], 5)
```

The cheapest designs sit right at the 0.75 line, and each estimate comes
from a finite number of simulations. With 1,000 simulations, the Monte
Carlo standard error of a power near 0.75 is
$\sqrt{0.75 \times 0.25 / 1000} \approx `r f3(sqrt(0.75 * 0.25 / 1000))`$.
Re-checking the three cheapest candidates with 5,000 simulations each:

```{r power-recheck}
top3 <- head(ok[order(ok$cost), ], 3)
set.seed(999)
top3$power_5000 <- mapply(estimate_power, top3$k, top3$s, MoreArgs = list(R = 5000))
top3$mc_se <- sqrt(top3$power_5000 * (1 - top3$power_5000) / 5000)
top3
```

Explore the design space in the widget. Each move of a slider simulates
one new monitoring program (left) and shows that design's estimated
power from the grid above (right).

```{r power-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("power_design.html")
```

> **Question:** Set $k = 10$ and $s = 4$, the cheapest design that
> meets the goal, and click "Simulate another program" ten times. How
> many of your programs detected the decline? Why is the answer for any
> single program so unpredictable, even when the power is 0.75?

## Discussion

1. The cheapest design ($k = 10$, $s = 4$, \$28,000) had estimated power
   `r f3(grid$power[grid$k == 10 & grid$s == 4])` from 1,000 simulations
   and `r f3(top3$power_5000[1])` from 5,000. The next design ($k = 11$,
   $s = 4$, \$29,400) came in at `r f3(top3$power_5000[2])`. Which would
   you recommend to the agency, and why?
2. Every check above used a case with a known answer: one person-day,
   a vector of two years, a stable population. Pick one function and
   describe a check you would add.
3. The simulation assumes the population declines smoothly, with all
   the year-to-year scatter coming from imperfect detection. Real
   populations also have good and bad years that carry over to the next
   year. How do you think that would change the power, and the
   false-decline rate?

## Bonus: prompting an AI assistant {#ai-prompts}

Code like this is a natural job for an AI assistant, as long as the
thinking (the model and the plan) comes first and every piece is
tested. Some pairs of prompts for the same task:

**The whole problem at once.**

- *Weak:* "Write R code for a power analysis for a declining toad
  population."
- *Better:* "Write an R function `estimate_power(k, s, R)` that calls my
  existing functions `simulate_counts(t_survey, k)` and
  `detect_decline(t_survey, counts)`. Survey years are
  `seq(1, 25, by = s)`. For each of `R` replicates, simulate new counts
  and record whether a decline was detected. Return the fraction
  detected. Base R only."
- The weak prompt leaves the model unstated, so the assistant fills it
  in with its own defaults (a canned $t$-test, a power package, a
  different noise model). The code may run and still answer a different
  question.

**Words or equations.**

- *Weak:* "Simulate survey counts for a population that declines 25%
  over 25 years with imperfect detection."
- *Better:* give the equations: $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$, detection
  probability $1 - (1 - p_{obs})^k$, and each count
  Binomial($N_t$ rounded, detection probability), one per survey year.
- "Declines 25%" could mean a straight-line or an exponential decline,
  and "imperfect detection" can be modeled many ways.

**Debugging.**

- *Weak:* "Fix my code." (with the whole script pasted)
- *Better:* "This function should return 25 counts, but
  `length(simulate_counts(1:25, 3))` returns 1. Here is the function.
  Explain why before suggesting a fix."
- A symptom, the expected behavior, and a short example make the
  problem checkable, and asking for an explanation first means you learn
  what went wrong.

**Testing.**

- *Weak:* "Is this code correct?"
- *Better:* "Write three tests for `detect_decline()` with known answers:
  a clearly declining series should return `TRUE`, and flat and
  increasing series should return `FALSE`."
- "Is this correct?" usually gets a confident yes. Check AI-written
  tests too: a test that compares a function with itself always passes.

**Leading questions.**

- *Weak:* "Show that survey frequency matters more than effort per
  survey."
- *Better:* "Compute power for $k = 1, \ldots, 15$ and $s = 1, \ldots, 5$
  and plot it, one line per $s$."
- Ask for the computation and interpret it yourself.

Some general habits for writing code with an assistant:

- Work out the model and the steps on paper first. The assistant is
  good at turning a clear plan into code and poor at choosing the right
  model for your question.
- Decide your checks before you see any code, and run them afterward:
  lengths, edge cases, and scenarios with a known answer.
- Ask one function at a time, with its inputs, output, and equations.
- Read the code before running it, and ask the assistant to explain
  anything you couldn't explain to a classmate.
- Don't paste sensitive data (unpublished data, locations of sensitive
  species); use a small made-up example with the same structure.
- Keep track of where AI helped, and say so in your own work.
